Chapter Eight: The Challenge of Forgiveness—Encounters with the Past
Forgiveness, the sisters realized, isn’t just a one-time act—it’s something you choose, again and again, every single day.
Think about it: the world around them was full of reminders of everything they’d lost. A glance at a stranger’s face, a name in the newspaper, even a memory that slipped in out of nowhere.
There were days when the anger just bubbled up—when the injustice of it all seemed impossible to carry.
But whenever that happened, the sisters always came back to what they learned in the camp: hatred just keeps the wounds open, while forgiveness is the only way to find real freedom.
One afternoon, something happened that would test everything they believed.
A man showed up at their door. There was something about his face that made their hearts skip—it was hauntingly familiar.
He’d been a guard at the camp, one of those men who enforced the rules, sometimes with cold indifference, sometimes with outright cruelty.
Now, he was standing in front of them—looking broken, full of shame—and he asked for their forgiveness.
In that moment, the air was thick with emotion: fear, anger, and even a hint of compassion all tangled together.
The sisters hesitated. The pain was still fresh, the scars just beneath the surface.
But as they looked at this man, they realized he wasn’t a monster. He was just another human, lost, desperate for a bit of grace.
That’s when it hit them—forgiveness isn’t about pretending the past didn’t hurt. It’s about making sure the past doesn’t trap you forever.
With trembling hands, they chose to offer him forgiveness. And in that moment, both sides—those who forgave, and the one who was forgiven—were changed.
Encounters like this didn’t happen often, but wow, did they leave a mark.
Each time, the sisters were reminded: forgiveness isn’t a place you arrive at—it’s an ongoing journey.
It takes real bravery, a bit of humility, and a willingness to see the humanity even in people who’ve done you harm.
Most of us will never face our enemies the way the sisters did. But sooner or later, we all have to figure out how to let go of the pain others have caused us.
The biggest lesson? Forgiveness isn’t just a feeling—it’s a choice. A decision to loosen the grip of anger and resentment on your heart.
It’s a gift, not just to the person you forgive, but to yourself.
And honestly, it’s the only way to truly start fresh.
